audits.question: Check the entry's rn/name-efficacy or mdw-ntr language/divinity link against an identifiable text or scholarly passage; do not make every receipt a spell or treat an English gloss as a complete theology.
audits.entry_locator: corpus/knowledge/civilizations/egypt-ancient.md §3, line 60 (mdw-nṯr sentence, with cross-reference to R93 pp. 35–36); related caution context §9 lines 169–172 (name transmission vs. name efficacy; R93 pp. 35–40 on words, actions, material properties).
audits.entry_claim: The entry asserts that Egyptian mdw-nṯr is conventionally glossed "god's words" and that this expression connects writing to divinity, while explicitly warning that not every surviving receipt is therefore a spell; it states that Ritner (R93) pp. 35–36 discuss the ritual use of the same expression.
audits.source_citation: Robert K. Ritner, The Mechanics of Ancient Egyptian Magical Practice, Studies in Ancient Oriental Civilization 54, Oriental Institute, University of Chicago; corrected 4th printing (2008), p. 35 (section "Magic as Speech, Property, and Rite," with nn. 160–162), continuing onto p. 36.
audits.source_locator: Printed p. 35 (verified from the page header "THE VOCABULARY OF MAGIC 35" in the ISAC open-access 4th-printing PDF, PDF page 53 of 340): the sentence naming Thoth "Lord of hieroglyphs" (nb mdw-ntr) and the sentence "Spells are specifically labeled as 'god's words' (mdw-ntr)", with n. 161 citing the rubric dd mdw-ntr (hr), "divine words to be said over ...", Harris Magical Papyrus cols. 6/8 and 9/12 (Lange 1927, pp. 51, 80; Sauneron 1970, pp. 10, 12); the discussion continues on printed p. 36.
audits.source_excerpt: Thus Thoth, the god of writing, is regularly qualified as 'excellent of magic' (mnh hkꜣ) in his capacity as 'Lord of hieroglyphs' (nb mdw-ntr). Spells are specifically labeled as 'god's words' (mdw-ntr)
audits.retrieval_method: Open-access PDF of the cited corrected 4th printing downloaded via the link published on the ISAC (Oriental Institute) publication page https://isac.uchicago.edu/research/publications/saoc/saoc-54-mechanics-ancient-egyptian-magical-practice-fourth-printing-2008 (the entry's own R93 link); text extracted with pdftotext -layout; printed folios confirmed from in-page headers. Working text kept only in the worker scratch reports/supplement-opencode-1/scratch/round6-03/; no raw download enters the corpus.
audits.basis: Mapped the bounded entry sentence onto the retrieved printed page: (1) the conventional gloss "god's words" for mdw-ntr is Ritner's own rendering, so the entry does not manufacture the English gloss; (2) the writing–divinity link is attested through Thoth's epithet nb mdw-ntr and through the ritual rubric dd mdw-ntr "divine words to be said over ..." (n. 161), which is exactly the "ritual use of the same expression" the entry attributes to R93 pp. 35–36; (3) the entry's caution that not every receipt is a spell agrees with Ritner's framing on the same page, where magic's "intrinsic association ... with word" is named the root of "modern Egyptology's obsession with the spell as the sine qua non of magic" while magic is analyzed as tripartite — property, rite, and speech — matching the entry's separate statement (R93 pp. 35–40) that heka is not speech alone. The citation's printed-page locator is accurate.
audits.coupling_implication: mdw-n᯿r's divinity link operates through specific institutions — Thoth's scribal epithets and spell rubrics — not through a blanket sanctity of all texts; a worldbuilding design should label which speech acts are mdw-nṯr-class rather than sacralize every document, and the English gloss must stay a citation form, not a recovered theology or vocalization.
audits.limits: English gloss and transliteration remain conventional scholarly renderings, not ancient pronunciation or a complete theology — the entry itself carries this warning and the audit does not upgrade the gloss. The clause "not every surviving receipt is a spell" is an entry-side interpretive guard; the page supports its spirit (Ritner explicitly de-centers the spell within magic) but a caution is not an independently provable historical proposition. The PDF's OCR garbles Egyptian transliteration in this passage (ḥkꜣ appears as "hk?", mnh as "mni/mnlh" in the footnote); excerpts above are from the English text lines, with sign readings left to the printed edition. Footnote 161's underlying Harris Magical Papyrus columns (Lange/Sauneron editions) were not themselves re-inspected; only Ritner's citation of them was. A14's Lesson 1 excerpt PDF (entry's own link) contains no retrievable mdw-ntr passage in pp. 1–10, so A14 corroborates this specific sentence only bibliographically.

audits.question: Check one explicit linen/pleating or garment-status claim using a dated material object or technical source; separate artistic convention, surviving textile and a complete cutting/pleating reconstruction.
audits.entry_locator: corpus/knowledge/civilizations/egypt-ancient.md §8, line 147 (Louvre tunic E 12026 object-level check); consistent with §6, line 110 ("surviving pleated linen already blocks 'pleats invented in the New Kingdom'") and §8 line 143 caution column citing Galczynski 2024 on "wool abhorrence".
audits.entry_claim: The entry asserts that Louvre tunic E 12026 supplies an object-level check: linen in plain weave with pleated sleeves and body, from Assiut tomb 13, catalogued late Dynasty 11–early Dynasty 12, and therefore pleating cannot safely function as an exclusively New Kingdom date-marker.
audits.source_citation: Musée du Louvre, collections database record for inv. E 12026 / IF 10-14, "tunique", Département des Antiquités égyptiennes; record last updated 28.03.2026, with the museum's own caveat that the contents do not necessarily take account of the latest data.
audits.source_locator: Record fields as displayed 2026-10-17: Description/Features "manches et corps plissés"; Materials and techniques "Matériau : lin", "Technique : toile"; Places and dates "Date: fin XIe dynastie ; début XIIe dynastie (contexte de fouilles) (-2045 - -1856)", "Place of discovery: tombe 13 (Assiout -> Moyenne Égypte -> Égypte)", discovery 27 February–end of May 1903 (Chassinat/Palanque excavation, partage 1903); dimensions H. 121 cm × W. 57 cm.
audits.source_excerpt: Matériau : lin ; Technique : toile ; manches et corps plissés ; Place of discovery : tombe 13 (Assiout) ; fin XIe dynastie ; début XIIe dynastie (contexte de fouilles) (-2045 - -1856)
audits.retrieval_method: Live FetchURL of the Louvre collections page for ark cl010005890 (HTML text extraction), 2026-10-17; field values quoted from the returned record text (French fields retained verbatim).
audits.basis: Every attribute of the entry's object-level sentence maps onto a retrieved record field: linen (lin), plain weave (toile), pleated sleeves and body (manches et corps plissés), findspot Assiut tomb 13, and catalogue dating fin XIe dynastie ; début XIIe dynastie (contexte de fouilles), −2045/−1856. The excavated, dated Middle Kingdom pleated linen tunic is direct material evidence that pleating predates the New Kingdom, grounding the entry's warning that pleating cannot serve as an exclusively New Kingdom date-marker. The record's own bibliography independently corroborates two entry-adjacent identifications: Vogelsang-Eastwood 1993, Pharaonic Egyptian Clothing, pl. 30 (the entry's VE93 plate locator) and Janssen 2020, "The Pleated Dress of Nywty", PalArch's Journal of Archaeology of Egypt/Egyptology 17, p. 7.
audits.coupling_implication: Pleated elite display rests on a surviving textile chain — flax processing to pleating and maintenance — already attested before the New Kingdom, so costume-based period inference must weigh excavated textiles against depicted silhouettes; the artifact separates the surviving object (this record) from both artistic convention (two-dimensional pleat rendering) and any complete cutting/pleating reconstruction, which the record does not supply.
audits.limits: The dating is the catalogue's attribution flagged "contexte de fouilles" (excavation context), not this audit's independent re-dating of the tomb group (Chassinat & Palanque 1911 publication not re-inspected); the record itself carries the museum caveat that it may not reflect the latest scholarship, which the entry faithfully repeats. The record documents the surviving textile's visible technique, not a full cutting or pleating-set reconstruction; the entry's separate caution that reconstruction remains interpretive (VE93) is consistent but was not itself newly verified here. Artistic-convention claims (how reliefs render pleats) are outside this record and were not tested. Record fields are in French; translations given above are this worker's.

R6-03-B_optional_bibliography_from_sourc: Vogelsang-Eastwood, G. M., Pharaonic Egyptian clothing, Leiden: E. J. Brill (Studies in Textile and Costume History 2), 1993, pl. 30 — listed in the retrieved Louvre record's bibliography, matching entry key VE93's plate locator.

Janssen, Rosalind M., "The Pleated Dress of Nywty", PalArch's Journal of Archaeology of Egypt/Egyptology 17 (2020), p. 1-11 (cited at p. 7) — listed in the retrieved record; not separately re-inspected in this audit.
